# Owl

> Owl is an object-graph database written in Rust. References between objects are part of the data model, so a query follows them with a dot instead of joining tables. It has its own query language, OQL, a storage engine with no other database underneath, and an HTTP server. It is under active development and not yet suitable for production data.

## The idea

If your data is already a graph of objects that point at each other, the database should let you query it that way. `orders.customer.name` is a path you walk, not a join you write.

## The language, OQL

A query starts from a collection and applies steps. The same steps work on a top-level collection, a list inside a document, and a relationship followed backwards.

```oql
orders
  .where { .status == "paid" }
  .sort { .total.desc }
  .limit(3)
  .select { id, who: .customer.name, total }
```

- Steps: `where`, `select`, `sort`, `limit`, `offset`, `group_by`, `having`, `count`, `sum`, `avg`, `min`, `max`, `first`, `nearest`.
- Forward reference: `.customer.name`. Reverse reference: `.orders` on a customer, derived from the schema with its own index.
- Recursion: `.walk(.children)` follows a relationship to any depth.
- Row positions: `partition_by`, `row_number()`, `rank()`, `prev()`, `so_far()`.
- Values enter a query as `$name` parameters and are never read as query text.

## Two forms of the same query

Every query can be written as a chain or as a block. They mean the same thing. A block can also name a value once and reuse it.

```oql
customers {
  paid = .orders.where { .status == "paid" }
  spent = paid.sum(.total)

  where { spent > 80 }
  select { name, orders: paid.count(), spent: spent }
}
```

## Functions

Functions are written in OQL and kept in the database. One can take a row, a value or a whole collection, and can return a value or a collection that chains like a built-in step.

```oql
fn spent(c: customers) {
  c.orders.where { .status == "paid" }.sum(.total)
}

customers.select { name, spent: spent(*) }
```

## Writing data and rules

```oql
customers.insert { id: "chen", name: "Chen", email: "chen@shop.test" }
products.where { .id == "kettle" && .stock > 0 }.update { stock -= 1 }
customers.upsert on id { id: "chen", name: "Chen W." }
orders.where { .status == "cancelled" }.delete()
```

A schema declares its rules: `unique`, `check(.price >= 0)`, `Ref(customers)` and `on delete cascade`. Owl refuses any write that would break one. A single statement is atomic, and a `transaction { ... }` block makes several statements succeed or fail together.

## The engine

- Every object has a stable 64-bit identity that is not a file position, so data can move without rewriting references.
- Records are compiled from the schema: field names are stored once, and a query decodes only the fields it asks for.
- Every commit is checksummed and synced to a write-ahead log; recovery loads the last checkpoint and replays the rest.
- Indexes: ordered, unique, composite, a reverse index for every reference, and vector search.

## What Owl is not, today

- It runs on one machine. The clustering code is experimental.
- Writes are applied one at a time.
- It has no syntax yet for changing a schema.

## Running it

```bash
cargo run --release -p owl-server -- --data shop.owl
curl 127.0.0.1:7878/v1/query --json '{"query": "orders.count()"}'
```
